Roughly speaking, a process satisfies the Markov property if one can make predictions for the future of the process based solely on its present state just as well as one could knowing the process's full history, hence independently from such history; i.e., conditional on the present state of the system, its future and past states are independent.

A Markov chain is a type of Markov process that has either discrete state space or discrete index set (often representing time), but the precise definition of a Markov chain varies.[3] For example, it is common to define a Markov chain as a Markov process in either discrete or continuous time with a countable state space (thus regardless of the nature of time),[4][5][6][7] but it is also common to define a Markov chain as having discrete time in either countable or continuous state space (thus regardless of the state space).[3]

Markov studied Markov processes in the early 20th century, publishing his first paper on the topic in 1906, but earlier uses of Markov processes already existed.[8][9][10]Random walks on the integers and the Gambler's ruin problem are examples of Markov processes[11][12] and were studied hundreds of years earlier.[13][14] Two important examples of Markov processes are the Wiener process, also known as the Brownian motion process, and the Poisson process,[15] which are considered the most important and central stochastic processes in the theory of stochastic processes,[16][17][18] and were discovered repeatedly and independently, both before and after 1906, in various settings.[19][20] These two processes are Markov processes in continuous time, while random walks on the integers and the Gambler's ruin problem are examples of Markov processes in discrete time.[11][12]

The adjective Markovian is used to describe something that is related to a Markov process.[29]

A diagram representing a two-state Markov process, with the states labelled E and A. Each number represents the probability of the Markov process changing from one state to another state, with the direction indicated by the arrow. For example, if the Markov process is in state A, then the probability it changes to state E is 0.4, while the probability it remains in state A is 0.6.

Introduction

A Markov chain is a stochastic process with the Markov property. The term "Markov chain" refers to the sequence of random variables such a process moves through, with the Markov property defining serial dependence only between adjacent periods (as in a "chain"). It can thus be used for describing systems that follow a chain of linked events, where what happens next depends only on the current state of the system.

The system's state space and time parameter index need to be specified. The following table gives an overview of the different instances of Markov processes for different levels of state space generality and for discrete time v. continuous time:

Note that there is no definitive agreement in the literature on the use of some of the terms that signify special cases of Markov processes. Usually the term "Markov chain" is reserved for a process with a discrete set of times, i.e. a discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC),[30][30] but a few authors use the term "Markov process" to refer to a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) without explicit mention.[31][32][33] In addition, there are other extensions of Markov processes that are referred to as such but do not necessarily fall within any of these four categories (see Markov model). Moreover, the time index need not necessarily be real-valued; like with the state space, there are conceivable processes that move through index sets with other mathematical constructs. Notice that the general state space continuous-time Markov chain is general to such a degree that it has no designated term.

While the time parameter is usually discrete, the state space of a Markov chain does not have any generally agreed-on restrictions: the term may refer to a process on an arbitrary state space.[34] However, many applications of Markov chains employ finite or countably infinite state spaces, which have a more straightforward statistical analysis. Besides time-index and state-space parameters, there are many other variations, extensions and generalizations (see Variations). For simplicity, most of this article concentrates on the discrete-time, discrete state-space case, unless mentioned otherwise.

The changes of state of the system are called transitions. The probabilities associated with various state changes are called transition probabilities. The process is characterized by a state space, a transition matrix describing the probabilities of particular transitions, and an initial state (or initial distribution) across the state space. By convention, we assume all possible states and transitions have been included in the definition of the process, so there is always a next state, and the process does not terminate.

A discrete-time random process involves a system which is in a certain state at each step, with the state changing randomly between steps. The steps are often thought of as moments in time, but they can equally well refer to physical distance or any other discrete measurement. Formally, the steps are the integers or natural numbers, and the random process is a mapping of these to states. The Markov property states that the conditional probability distribution for the system at the next step (and in fact at all future steps) depends only on the current state of the system, and not additionally on the state of the system at previous steps.

Since the system changes randomly, it is generally impossible to predict with certainty the state of a Markov chain at a given point in the future. However, the statistical properties of the system's future can be predicted. In many applications, it is these statistical properties that are important.

A famous Markov chain is the so-called "drunkard's walk", a random walk on the number line where, at each step, the position may change by +1 or -1 with equal probability. From any position there are two possible transitions, to the next or previous integer. The transition probabilities depend only on the current position, not on the manner in which the position was reached. For example, the transition probabilities from 5 to 4 and 5 to 6 are both 0.5, and all other transition probabilities from 5 are 0. These probabilities are independent of whether the system was previously in 4 or 6.

Another example is the dietary habits of a creature who eats only grapes, cheese, or lettuce, and whose dietary habits conform to the following rules:

It eats exactly once a day.

If it ate cheese today, tomorrow it will eat lettuce or grapes with equal probability.

If it ate grapes today, tomorrow it will eat grapes with probability 1/10, cheese with probability 4/10 and lettuce with probability 5/10.

If it ate lettuce today, tomorrow it will eat grapes with probability 4/10 or cheese with probability 6/10. It will not eat lettuce again tomorrow.

This creature's eating habits can be modeled with a Markov chain since its choice tomorrow depends solely on what it ate today, not what it ate yesterday or any other time in the past. One statistical property that could be calculated is the expected percentage, over a long period, of the days on which the creature will eat grapes.

A series of independent events (for example, a series of coin flips) satisfies the formal definition of a Markov chain. However, the theory is usually applied only when the probability distribution of the next step depends non-trivially on the current state.

History

Andrey Markov studied Markov chains in the early 20th century. Markov was interested in studying an extension of independent random sequences, motivated by a disagreement with Pavel Nekrasov who claimed independence was necessary for the weak law of large numbers to hold.[35] In his first paper on Markov chains, published in 1906, Markov showed that under certain conditions the average outcomes of the Markov chain would converge to a fixed vector of values, so proving a weak law of large numbers without the independence assumption,[8][9][10] which had been commonly regarded as a requirement for such mathematical laws to hold.[10] Markov later used Markov chains to study the distribution of vowels in Eugene Onegin, written by Alexander Pushkin, and proved a central limit theorem for such chains.[8]

In 1912 Poincaré studied Markov chains on finite groups with an aim to study card shuffling. Other early uses of Markov chains include a diffusion model, introduced by Paul and Tatyana Ehrenfest in 1907, and a branching process, introduced by Francis Galton and Henry William Watson in 1873, preceding the work of Markov.[8][9] After the work of Galton and Watson, it was later revealed that their branching process had been independently discovered and studied around three decades earlier by Irénée-Jules Bienaymé.[36] Starting in 1928, Maurice Fréchet became interested in Markov chains, eventually resulting in him publishing in 1938 a detailed study on Markov chains.[8][37]

Andrei Kolmogorov developed in a 1931 paper a large part of the early theory of continuous-time Markov processes.[38][39] Kolmogorov was partly inspired by Louis Bachelier's 1900 work on fluctuations in the stock market as well as Norbert Wiener's work on Einstein's model of Brownian movement.[38][40] He introduced and studied a particular set of Markov processes known as diffusion processes, where he derived a set of differential equations describing the processes.[38][41] Independent of Kolmgorov's work, Sydney Chapman derived in a 1928 paper an equation, now called the Chapman-Kolmogorov equation, in a less mathematically rigorous way than Kolmogorov, while studying Brownian movement.[42] The differential equations are now called the Kolmogorov equations[43] or the Kolmogorov-Chapman equations.[44] Other mathematicians who contributed significantly to the foundations of Markov processes include William Feller, starting in 1930s, and then later Eugene Dynkin, starting in the 1950s.[39]

Examples

Gambling

Suppose that you start with $10, and you wager $1 on an unending, fair, coin toss indefinitely, or until you lose all of your money. If Xn{\displaystyle X_{n}} represents the number of dollars you have after n tosses, with X0=10{\displaystyle X_{0}=10}, then the sequence {Xn:n∈N}{\displaystyle \{X_{n}:n\in \mathbb {N} \}} is a Markov process. If I know that you have $12 now, then it would be expected that with even odds, you will either have $11 or $13 after the next toss. This guess is not improved by the added knowledge that you started with $10, then went up to $11, down to $10, up to $11, and then to $12.

The process described here is a Markov chain on a countable state space that follows a random walk.

A birth-death process

If one pops one hundred kernels of popcorn, each kernel popping at an independent exponentially-distributed time, then this would be a continuous-time Markov process. If Xt{\displaystyle X_{t}} denotes the number of kernels which have popped up to time t, the problem can be defined as finding the number of kernels that will pop in some later time. The only thing one needs to know is the number of kernels that have popped prior to the time "t". It is not necessary to know when they popped, so knowing Xt{\displaystyle X_{t}} for previous times "t" is not relevant.

The process described here is an approximation of a Poisson point process - Poisson processes are also Markov processes.

A non-Markov example

Suppose that you have a coin purse containing five quarters (each worth 25c), five nickels (each worth 5c) and five dimes (each worth 10c), and one-by-one, you randomly draw coins from the purse and set them on a table. If Xn{\displaystyle X_{n}} represents the total value of the coins set on the table after n draws, with X0=0{\displaystyle X_{0}=0}, then the sequence {Xn:n∈N}{\displaystyle \{X_{n}:n\in \mathbb {N} \}} is not a Markov process.

Answer: It presents an introduction to the basic elements in probability and focuses on two main areas: elementary probability and Markov Chains", "truncated": false, "original_chars": 4181, "returned_chars": 4181}, {"rank": 6, "id": "shard_02763_31458", "docid": "shard_02763_31458", "kind": "document", "rrf_score": 0.016129, "text": "In the early 20th century, Russian mathematician Andrey Markov made significant contributions to the field of probability theory through his work on stochastic processes, which eventually led to the development of what we now know as Markov chains. These mathematical models allow us to describe systems where future states depend only on the present state and not on how we arrived at it – a property known as the Markov property. This breakthrough has had far-reaching implications across various disciplines such as physics, chemistry, economics, linguistics, computer science, and engineering.

Markov began developing these ideas around 1906 when he published his first paper introducing the concept of 'chain kinship', focusing on sequences of vowels and consonants in the works of Alexander Pushkin. He later refined this notion by defining more general conditions under which statistical dependence between successive elements becomes negligible. This paved the way for modern information theory, particularly with regards to data compression and communication channels.

A simple random process can illustrate the essence of a Markov chain. Imagine flipping a biased coin repeatedly; let's say heads results in continuing to flip the same coin (state H), whereas tails means switching to a fair coin (state F). The outcome of each toss depends solely on the type of coin being used at that moment; hence, this forms a two-state Markov chain. We denote transition probabilities from one state to another using matrices:

P = | Probability(H|H) Probability(F|H) |
| Probability(H|F) Probability(F|F) |
= | p q |
| r s |

Here, p represents the likelihood of getting heads given that the previous result was also heads; similarly, q denotes the chance of switching to the fair coin after flipping heads. Likewise, r stands for the probability of remaining at the fair coin after previously landing on it, and s signifies returning to the biased coin post-flip. It's important to note that all entries in matrix P must lie within the interval [0,1], and row sums should equal 1 due to probability normalization constraints.

The power of the Markov property lies in its ability to predict future behavior based on current knowledge alone. Given the initial distribution vector π^0 over our system's possible states, subsequent distributions π^n can be calculated iteratively via multiplication with the transition probability matrix P raised to increasing powers n:

π^n = π^0 * P^n

This recursion captures the inherent memoryless nature of Markov chains since past states do not influence future ones beyond their contribution to the present state.

In summary, Andrey Markov laid the foundation for modern information theory through his groundbreaking work on stochastic processes and Markov chains. By modeling complex systems as finite sets of interconnected states governed by fixed transition probabilities, researchers gained valuable insights into understanding patterns, trends, and predictions. As we conclude this textbook on Modern Markov Chain Theory, it is worth taking some time to reflect on the state of the field and consider possible avenues for future research. The study of Markov chains has a rich history dating back over a century, and yet there remain many open questions and exciting opportunities for exploration.

One area where significant progress has been made in recent years is in the development of efficient algorithms for simulating and analyzing Markov chain dynamics. This includes both theoretical advances in our understanding of convergence rates and mixing times, as well as practical methods for implementing these ideas in software packages. However, there is still much work to be done in order to develop more sophisticated tools for handling complex systems, such as those arising in machine learning or statistical physics. One promising direction involves the use of tensor networks and other numerical methods to efficiently approximate high-dimensional distributions and transition kernels (see e.g., [1]).

Another active area of research concerns the application of Markov chains to various problems in data science, including clustering, dimensionality reduction, and feature selection. Here, one important challenge is to develop rigorous theoretical guarantees for these methods, which often rely on heuristics or ad hoc procedures. Recent work in this vein has focused on establishing connections between Markov chains and topics such as optimal transport, information theory, and convex optimization (see e.g., [2],[3]). These insights may help pave the way towards a more principled approach to designing and analyzing Markov chain algorithms for modern data analysis tasks.

A third frontier for Markov chain research lies at the intersection of probability theory and mathematical physics. Over the past few decades, there has been growing interest in understanding how concepts from statistical mechanics can be applied to study the behavior of large random structures, such as spin glasses, disordered systems, and random graphs. Markov chains play an essential role in many of these models, providing a powerful tool for exploring their collective properties and phase transitions. Nevertheless, several fundamental questions remain unanswered, particularly when it comes to developing precise asymptotic estimates or proving sharp thresholds for various phenomena (see e.g., [4],[5]). Further progress in this area will likely require the combined efforts of probabilists, physicists, and computer scientists working together to tackle these challenges.

Beyond these broad themes, there are also numerous specific open problems and conjectures scattered throughout the literature on Markov chains. Some of these concern basic issues in the foundations of the subject, such as determining whether certain classes of chains admit cutoff phenomena or rapid mixing rates under natural conditions (see e.g., [6],[7]). Others involve more specialized topics, such as the analysis of random walks on groups, the study of interacting particle systems, or the investigation of non-reversible Markov chains (see e.g., [8],[9],[10]). Tackling any one of these questions would represent a valuable contribution to our understanding of this venerable and fascinating subject.

In conclusion, the field of Markov chain theory remains an incredibly vibrant and dynamic area of research, with ample opportunities for innovation and discovery. By building upon the firm foundation laid by previous generations of scholars, we can continue to push the boundaries of what is known and explore new realms of applicability for these versatile mathematical objects. We hope that this textbook has provided a useful introduction to the core concepts and techniques in the subject, and that it will inspire readers to join us in pursuing these exciting endeavors.

10.1 Introduction

In the realm of discrete mathematics, combinatorics stands out as a captivating branch that deals with counting, arranging, and combining objects according to certain rules. While it may seem abstract and detached from reality at first glance, combinatorics finds itself at the heart of numerous practical applications, particularly in the fight against diseases. This chapter will delve into the intricacies of combinatorial methods and their significance in modern epidemiology. We will explore how these techniques aid in modeling complex systems, analyzing patterns, and predicting outcomes, ultimately contributing to informed decision-making during public health crises. So let us embark on this fascinating journey where seemingly unrelated worlds collide - the elegance of mathematics and the urgency of global health challenges.

10.2 Foundations of Combinatorics

Before diving into advanced topics, it's crucial to establish a solid foundation by introducing essential terminologies and fundamental principles of combinatorics. These building blocks include permutations, combinations, and binomial coefficients, which are integral components of more sophisticated methods employed in disease modeling.

10.2.1 Permutations

Permutation refers to the arrangement of items from a given set, usually distinct elements arranged in a particular order. Given a set S = {a, b, c}, there exist six possible permutations: (a,b,c), (a,c,b), (b,a,c), (b,c,a), (c,a,b), and (c,b,a). In general, if n denotes the number of elements in a set, then the total number of permutations can be calculated using the formula P(n) = n!, where ! represents factorial, i.e., the product of all positive integers up to n.

10.2.2 Combinations

Unlike permutations, combinations deal with selecting subsets without considering their ordering. For instance, when choosing two colors from a palette containing red, blue, green, and yellow, the combination {red, blue} is equivalent to {blue, red}. To compute the total number of k-combinations from a set containing n elements, mathematicians employ the binomial coefficient notation C(n,k) or nCk, defined as follows:

nCk = n! / [k!(n-k)!]

Here, k signifies the size of the desired subset. It's worth noting that the term "binomial coefficient" stems from its appearance in the expansion of powers of binomials like (x+y)^n.

10.3 Graph Theory and Network Analysis

Graph theory, another vital aspect of combinatorics, offers powerful tools for representing relationships between entities as networks. In this section, we will explore stationary times through the lens of Markov chains, which we introduced earlier in the chapter. Specifically, we will focus on discrete-time Markov chains, which are mathematical models used to describe systems that transition between states based on fixed probabilities. We will also assume that these Markov chains are finite, meaning they only have finitely many possible states.

First, let's define some terms. A state space is the set of all possible states that our system can occupy at any given time. A transition matrix describes the probabilities of moving from one state to another. Finally, an initial distribution specifies the starting state or the likelihood of beginning in each state.

Now, suppose we have a discrete-time Markov chain with a single recurrent class (a group of communicating states such that once the chain enters this class, it never leaves). By definition, there exists at least one state within this class that returns to itself infinitely often as time goes on. Let's call this special state the "root." Furthermore, let's denote by $f\_i$ the expected number of steps required for the chain to return to the root starting from state $i$. These values are known as mean first passage times.

With this background established, we can finally define what we mean by a stationary time. Given a state $i$, a stopping time $\tau$ is said to be stationary if it satisfies the following conditions:

1. The event ${\{\tau = n\}}$ depends only on the $(n-1)^{th}$ step of the Markov chain.
	* Intuitively, this means that the decision to stop must depend solely on the present state, not on past history.
2. If ${\tau > n}$, then ${X\_n \neq i}$.
	* Once the chain reaches state $i$, we decide immediately whether or not to stop.

The main result we want to establish regarding stationary times concerns their expected value. Suppose we choose a stationary time uniformly at random from $\{0, 1, ..., f\_i\}$; that is, every integer in this range has equal probability of being selected. Then, the expected value of this random variable equals precisely $f\_i / 2$.

To prove this statement, consider constructing a directed graph whose vertices correspond to the elements of the recurrent class containing $i$. Each edge points from state $j$ to state $k$ whenever the probability of transitioning directly from $j$ to $k$ is nonzero. Since there are no absorbing states (as defined previously), this graph must contain at least one cycle. Choose such a cycle and fix any vertex within it.

Next, observe that since the chosen cycle forms a closed path, it follows that the sum of the entries along any row of the transition matrix corresponding to a state within the cycle remains constant regardless of the position of that row relative to other rows. Consequently, we may rearrange the rows of the transition matrix so that those belonging to the cycle appear together consecutively. Denote by $M'$ the resulting submatrix.

Since the determinant of a square matrix is invariant under cyclic permutations of its rows, it must hold that $|\det M'|=1$. However, because each entry of $M'$ lies strictly between zero and one, it cannot be invertible over the real numbers. Therefore, $M'$ must possess an eigenvalue exactly equal to unity.

Let $\pi$ denote the left eigenvector associated with this eigenvalue. Note that $\pi$ necessarily sums to one due to normalization requirements. One important application of card shuffling processes lies in the study of random walks and mixing times. As we conclude this textbook on Modern Markov Chain Theory, it is worth taking some time to reflect on the state of the field and consider possible avenues for future research. The study of Markov chains has a rich history dating back over a century, and yet there remain many open questions and exciting opportunities for exploration.

One area where significant progress has been made in recent years is in the development of efficient algorithms for simulating and analyzing Markov chain dynamics. This includes both theoretical advances in our understanding of convergence rates and mixing times, as well as practical methods for implementing these ideas in software packages. However, there is still much work to be done in order to develop more sophisticated tools for handling complex systems, such as those arising in machine learning or statistical physics. One promising direction involves the use of tensor networks and other numerical methods to efficiently approximate high-dimensional distributions and transition kernels (see e.g., [1]).

Another active area of research concerns the application of Markov chains to various problems in data science, including clustering, dimensionality reduction, and feature selection. Here, one important challenge is to develop rigorous theoretical guarantees for these methods, which often rely on heuristics or ad hoc procedures. Recent work in this vein has focused on establishing connections between Markov chains and topics such as optimal transport, information theory, and convex optimization (see e.g., [2],[3]). These insights may help pave the way towards a more principled approach to designing and analyzing Markov chain algorithms for modern data analysis tasks.

A third frontier for Markov chain research lies at the intersection of probability theory and mathematical physics. Over the past few decades, there has been growing interest in understanding how concepts from statistical mechanics can be applied to study the behavior of large random structures, such as spin glasses, disordered systems, and random graphs. Markov chains play an essential role in many of these models, providing a powerful tool for exploring their collective properties and phase transitions. Nevertheless, several fundamental questions remain unanswered, particularly when it comes to developing precise asymptotic estimates or proving sharp thresholds for various phenomena (see e.g., [4],[5]). Further progress in this area will likely require the combined efforts of probabilists, physicists, and computer scientists working together to tackle these challenges.

Beyond these broad themes, there are also numerous specific open problems and conjectures scattered throughout the literature on Markov chains. Some of these concern basic issues in the foundations of the subject, such as determining whether certain classes of chains admit cutoff phenomena or rapid mixing rates under natural conditions (see e.g., [6],[7]). Others involve more specialized topics, such as the analysis of random walks on groups, the study of interacting particle systems, or the investigation of non-reversible Markov chains (see e.g., [8],[9],[10]). Tackling any one of these questions would represent a valuable contribution to our understanding of this venerable and fascinating subject.

In conclusion, the field of Markov chain theory remains an incredibly vibrant and dynamic area of research, with ample opportunities for innovation and discovery. By building upon the firm foundation laid by previous generations of scholars, we can continue to push the boundaries of what is known and explore new realms of applicability for these versatile mathematical objects. We hope that this textbook has provided a useful introduction to the core concepts and techniques in the subject, and that it will inspire readers to join us in pursuing these exciting endeavors.

5.4.2 Queueing Theory

Another important application of Markov chains lies in modeling queues, such as those encountered in telecommunications or transportation networks. The celebrated Little's Law relates the average number of customers in a stable queue (L), the arrival rate (λ), and the service time distribution (μ) via L=λW, where W denotes the expected waiting time. No one else seems to have suggested the following approach. Suppose we keep flipping a coin until we get five heads in a row. Define a "run" as either five consecutive heads or a tails flip plus the preceding streak of heads flips. (A run could be a single tails flip.) The number of coin flips is equal to the number of runs with at least four heads ($R_{4+}$), plus the number of runs with at least three heads ($R_{3+}$), and so on down to the number of runs with at least zero heads ($R_{0+}$). We can see this by expanding the terms:

By linearity of expectation, the expected number of coin flips is $E(R_{0+}) + E(R_{1+}) + \ldots + E(R_{4+})$. $E(R_{4+})$ is $2 E(R_{5+}) = 2$, because one half of the time we flip at least four heads in a row, we go on to flip five heads in a row, i.e. the following coin flip is heads. In other words, in expectation, it takes two runs that start with four heads to achieve one run of five heads. Likewise, $E(R_{3+}) = 2 E(R_{4+}) = 4$, $E(R_{2+}) = 2 E(R_{3+}) = 8$, $E(R_{1+}) = 2 E(R_{2+}) = 16$, and $E(R_{0+}) = 2 E(R_{1+}) = 32$. The expected number of coin flips is $32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 62$.

More generally, given a biased coin that comes up heads $p$ portion of the time, the expected number of flips to get $n$ heads in a row is $\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p^2} + \ldots + \frac{1}{p^n} = \frac{1 - p^n}{p^n(1 - p)}$.

By definition, there exists at least one state within this class that returns to itself infinitely often as time goes on. Let's call this special state the "root." Furthermore, let's denote by $f\_i$ the expected number of steps required for the chain to return to the root starting from state $i$. These values are known as mean first passage times.

2. If ${\tau > n}$, then ${X\_n \neq i}$.
	* Once the chain reaches state $i$, we decide immediately whether or not to stop.

The main result we want to establish regarding stationary times concerns their expected value. Then, the expected value of this random variable equals precisely $f\_i / 2$.

To prove this statement, consider constructing a directed graph whose vertices correspond to the elements of the recurrent class containing $i$. Each edge points from state $j$ to state $k$ whenever the probability of transitioning directly from $j$ to $k$ is nonzero. Since there are no absorbing states (as defined previously), this graph must contain at least one cycle. Choose such a cycle and fix any vertex within it.

Markov chains are stochastic processes in which the conditional distribution of the next state depends on the present state but not on the earlier history, a property commonly called the Markov property. In a discrete-time chain, the model is specified by a state space, an initial distribution, and transition probabilities, often collected in a transition matrix whose entries describe the probability of moving from one state to another. The central simplification is not that the process is independent, but that its dependence can be compressed into a sufficiently informative present state. This idea connects probability with statistics because it permits long-run quantities such as stationary distributions, expected hitting times, and limiting averages to be studied even when observations are serially dependent. It connects probability with combinatorics because random walks on graphs, permutations, groups, and other discrete structures turn combinatorial questions into questions about transitions, convergence, and counting. The historical genesis of Markov chains arose partly from a dispute over whether independence was necessary for the weak law of large numbers. Andrey Markov’s first paper on the subject, published in 1906, showed under suitable conditions that averages along a dependent chain could still converge, thereby weakening the presumed need for independent trials. Markov subsequently used the method to study the distribution of vowels in Pushkin’s Eugene Onegin and to establish a central limit theorem for Markov-dependent sequences. Thus, the original motivation was not merely to model random motion but to extend statistical limit theory from independent observations to structured dependence. The framework also absorbed earlier problems, including random walks and gambler’s ruin, while later work extended it to card shuffling, diffusion, continuous-time processes, and branching phenomena. Contemporary research treats Markov chains both as mathematical objects whose convergence must be understood and as computational mechanisms for exploring distributions that cannot be handled analytically. A finite irreducible and aperiodic chain has a unique stationary distribution, and its distribution after many transitions converges to that stationary distribution regardless of its starting state. The mixing time measures how long the chain takes to become approximately stationary, and modern research often studies how that time grows as the underlying graph, combinatorial object, or state space becomes large. Important analytical tools include coupling, eigenvalue and spectral-gap methods, conductance, strong stationary times, and comparisons between random walks and electrical networks. These methods allow researchers to distinguish rapidly mixing chains, which become useful computationally, from chains that remain trapped for long periods in particular regions of the state space. In algebraic and enumerative combinatorics, random walks on permutations and groups support the analysis of card shuffling, while random walks on graphs reveal geometric properties such as bottlenecks and expansion. A notable example is riffle shuffling, for which the mixing-time analysis shows that seven shuffles are sufficient to make an ordinary 52-card deck approximately random under a standard distance criterion. Markov chains also provide randomized algorithms for approximate counting, including counting graph colourings, where proving a polynomially bounded mixing time supplies a theoretical justification for the algorithm’s efficiency. In statistics, Markov chain Monte Carlo constructs a chain whose stationary distribution is the target posterior distribution, allowing expectations and other posterior quantities to be approximated from dependent samples. The Metropolis and Metropolis–Hastings algorithms propose moves and accept or reject them so that the resulting chain converges to the desired distribution, while Gibbs sampling updates coordinates from conditional distributions. This is especially valuable in Bayesian models whose posterior densities are too complicated to normalize or integrate directly, although high dimensionality, autocorrelation, and slow mixing can make computation difficult. Current research therefore focuses not only on constructing chains but also on proving convergence rates, diagnosing dependence, improving simulation algorithms, and handling large or structured state spaces. Applications extend across statistical physics, machine learning, data science, bioinformatics, engineering, random graphs, spin systems, approximate counting, and interacting particle systems. Open directions include sharper results for cutoff and rapid mixing, scalable methods for high-dimensional distributions, non-reversible chains, and principled links with optimal transport, information theory, and convex optimization. The expected number of flips needed to obtain N consecutive heads illustrates the Markov-chain method because the relevant state is the current length of the consecutive-head run, not the entire sequence of previous flips. Let E_j denote the expected additional number of flips when the current run contains j consecutive heads, for j from 0 through N, with E_N equal to zero because the target has been reached. For a coin with head probability p and tail probability q equal to 1 minus p, first-step analysis gives E_j equal to 1 plus pE_{j+1} plus qE_0 for j less than N. The term 1 counts the next flip, the pE_{j+1} term describes extending the run after a head, and the qE_0 term describes the complete reset caused by a tail. The reset is the key intuition: a tail does not merely remove one head from the current run, because the newly completed suffix contains no consecutive heads and the process returns to state 0. Solving these coupled equations gives E_0 equal to (1 minus p to the power N) divided by q times p to the power N. For a fair coin, p and q are both one-half, so the expected number of flips is E_0 equal to 2 to the power of N plus 1 minus 2, or equivalently 2 times (2 to the power of N minus 1). Consequently, one head requires two flips on average, two consecutive heads require six, three require fourteen, and five require sixty-two. The five-head case can also be represented as an absorbing Markov chain with transient states 0 through 4 and absorbing state 5, where the vector m of expected remaining times satisfies (I minus Q)m equal to the all-ones vector. This example shows why Markov chains are useful in statistics and combinatorics: a seemingly history-dependent problem becomes a finite system of linear equations once the state records exactly the information needed for the future.

Introduction

A Markov chain is a stochastic process with the Markov property. The term "Markov chain" refers to the sequence of random variables such a process moves through, with the Markov property defining serial dependence only between adjacent periods (as in a "chain"). It can thus be used for describing systems that follow a chain of linked events, where what happens next depends only on the current state of the system.

The system's state space and time parameter index need to be specified. The following table gives an overview of the different instances of Markov processes for different levels of state space generality and for discrete time v. continuous time:

Note that there is no definitive agreement in the literature on the use of some of the terms that signify special cases of Markov processes. Usually the term "Markov chain" is reserved for a process with a discrete set of times, i.e. a discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC),[30][30] but a few authors use the term "Markov process" to refer to a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) without explicit mention.[31][32][33] In addition, there are other extensions of Markov processes that are referred to as such but do not necessarily fall within any of these four categories (see Markov model). Moreover, the time index need not necessarily be real-valued; like with the state space, there are conceivable processes that move through index sets with other mathematical constructs. Notice that the general state space continuous-time Markov chain is general to such a degree that it has no designated term.

While the time parameter is usually discrete, the state space of a Markov chain does not have any generally agreed-on restrictions: the term may refer to a process on an arbitrary state space.[34] However, many applications of Markov chains employ finite or countably infinite state spaces, which have a more straightforward statistical analysis. Besides time-index and state-space parameters, there are many other variations, extensions and generalizations (see Variations). For simplicity, most of this article concentrates on the discrete-time, discrete state-space case, unless mentioned otherwise.

The changes of state of the system are called transitions. The probabilities associated with various state changes are called transition probabilities. The process is characterized by a state space, a transition matrix describing the probabilities of particular transitions, and an initial state (or initial distribution) across the state space. By convention, we assume all possible states and transitions have been included in the definition of the process, so there is always a next state, and the process does not terminate.

A discrete-time random process involves a system which is in a certain state at each step, with the state changing randomly between steps. The steps are often thought of as moments in time, but they can equally well refer to physical distance or any other discrete measurement. Formally, the steps are the integers or natural numbers, and the random process is a mapping of these to states. The Markov property states that the conditional probability distribution for the system at the next step (and in fact at all future steps) depends only on the current state of the system, and not additionally on the state of the system at previous steps.

Since the system changes randomly, it is generally impossible to predict with certainty the state of a Markov chain at a given point in the future. However, the statistical properties of the system's future can be predicted. In many applications, it is these statistical properties that are important.

A famous Markov chain is the so-called "drunkard's walk", a random walk on the number line where, at each step, the position may change by +1 or -1 with equal probability. From any position there are two possible transitions, to the next or previous integer. The transition probabilities depend only on the current position, not on the manner in which the position was reached. For example, the transition probabilities from 5 to 4 and 5 to 6 are both 0.5, and all other transition probabilities from 5 are 0. These probabilities are independent of whether the system was previously in 4 or 6.

Another example is the dietary habits of a creature who eats only grapes, cheese, or lettuce, and whose dietary habits conform to the following rules:

It eats exactly once a day.

If it ate cheese today, tomorrow it will eat lettuce or grapes with equal probability.

If it ate grapes today, tomorrow it will eat grapes with probability 1/10, cheese with probability 4/10 and lettuce with probability 5/10.

If it ate lettuce today, tomorrow it will eat grapes with probability 4/10 or cheese with probability 6/10. It will not eat lettuce again tomorrow.

This creature's eating habits can be modeled with a Markov chain since its choice tomorrow depends solely on what it ate today, not what it ate yesterday or any other time in the past. One statistical property that could be calculated is the expected percentage, over a long period, of the days on which the creature will eat grapes.

A series of independent events (for example, a series of coin flips) satisfies the formal definition of a Markov chain. However, the theory is usually applied only when the probability distribution of the next step depends non-trivially on the current state.

History

Andrey Markov studied Markov chains in the early 20th century. Markov was interested in studying an extension of independent random sequences, motivated by a disagreement with Pavel Nekrasov who claimed independence was necessary for the weak law of large numbers to hold.[35] In his first paper on Markov chains, published in 1906, Markov showed that under certain conditions the average outcomes of the Markov chain would converge to a fixed vector of values, so proving a weak law of large numbers without the independence assumption,[8][9][10] which had been commonly regarded as a requirement for such mathematical laws to hold.[10] Markov later used Markov chains to study the distribution of vowels in Eugene Onegin, written by Alexander Pushkin, and proved a central limit theorem for such chains.[8]

In 1912 Poincaré studied Markov chains on finite groups with an aim to study card shuffling. Other early uses of Markov chains include a diffusion model, introduced by Paul and Tatyana Ehrenfest in 1907, and a branching process, introduced by Francis Galton and Henry William Watson in 1873, preceding the work of Markov.[8][9] After the work of Galton and Watson, it was later revealed that their branching process had been independently discovered and studied around three decades earlier by Irénée-Jules Bienaymé.[36] Starting in 1928, Maurice Fréchet became interested in Markov chains, eventually resulting in him publishing in 1938 a detailed study on Markov chains.[8][37]

Andrei Kolmogorov developed in a 1931 paper a large part of the early theory of continuous-time Markov processes.[38][39] Kolmogorov was partly inspired by Louis Bachelier's 1900 work on fluctuations in the stock market as well as Norbert Wiener's work on Einstein's model of Brownian movement.[38][40] He introduced and studied a particular set of Markov processes known as diffusion processes, where he derived a set of differential equations describing the processes.[38][41] Independent of Kolmgorov's work, Sydney Chapman derived in a 1928 paper an equation, now called the Chapman-Kolmogorov equation, in a less mathematically rigorous way than Kolmogorov, while studying Brownian movement.[42] The differential equations are now called the Kolmogorov equations[43] or the Kolmogorov-Chapman equations.[44] Other mathematicians who contributed significantly to the foundations of Markov processes include William Feller, starting in 1930s, and then later Eugene Dynkin, starting in the 1950s.[39]

Gambling

Suppose that you start with $10, and you wager $1 on an unending, fair, coin toss indefinitely, or until you lose all of your money. If Xn{\displaystyle X_{n}} represents the number of dollars you have after n tosses, with X0=10{\displaystyle X_{0}=10}, then the sequence {Xn:n∈N}{\displaystyle \{X_{n}:n\in \mathbb {N} \}} is a Markov process. If I know that you have $12 now, then it would be expected that with even odds, you will either have $11 or $13 after the next toss. This guess is not improved by the added knowledge that you started with $10, then went up to $11, down to $10, up to $11, and then to $12.

The process described here is a Markov chain on a countable state space that follows a random walk.

A birth-death process

If one pops one hundred kernels of popcorn, each kernel popping at an independent exponentially-distributed time, then this would be a continuous-time Markov process. If Xt{\displaystyle X_{t}} denotes the number of kernels which have popped up to time t, the problem can be defined as finding the number of kernels that will pop in some later time. The only thing one needs to know is the number of kernels that have popped prior to the time "t". It is not necessary to know when they popped, so knowing Xt{\displaystyle X_{t}} for previous times "t" is not relevant.

The process described here is an approximation of a Poisson point process - Poisson processes are also Markov processes.

A non-Markov example

Suppose that you have a coin purse containing five quarters (each worth 25c), five nickels (each worth 5c) and five dimes (each worth 10c), and one-by-one, you randomly draw coins from the purse and set them on a table. Markov chains are stochastic processes in which the conditional distribution of the next state depends on the present state but not on the earlier history, a property commonly called the Markov property. [shard_06241_78978]

In a discrete-time chain, the model is specified by a state space, an initial distribution, and transition probabilities, often collected in a transition matrix whose entries describe the probability of moving from one state to another. [shard_06241_78978]

The central simplification is not that the process is independent, but that its dependence can be compressed into a sufficiently informative present state. [shard_06241_78978]

This idea connects probability with statistics because it permits long-run quantities such as stationary distributions, expected hitting times, and limiting averages to be studied even when observations are serially dependent. [shard_06241_78978] [shard_03951_21465]

It connects probability with combinatorics because random walks on graphs, permutations, groups, and other discrete structures turn combinatorial questions into questions about transitions, convergence, and counting. [shard_03951_21465] [shard_06372_3482]

The historical genesis of Markov chains arose partly from a dispute over whether independence was necessary for the weak law of large numbers. [shard_06241_78978]

Andrey Markov’s first paper on the subject, published in 1906, showed under suitable conditions that averages along a dependent chain could still converge, thereby weakening the presumed need for independent trials. [shard_06241_78978]

Markov subsequently used the method to study the distribution of vowels in Pushkin’s Eugene Onegin and to establish a central limit theorem for Markov-dependent sequences. [shard_06241_78978]

Thus, the original motivation was not merely to model random motion but to extend statistical limit theory from independent observations to structured dependence. [shard_06241_78978]

The framework also absorbed earlier problems, including random walks and gambler’s ruin, while later work extended it to card shuffling, diffusion, continuous-time processes, and branching phenomena. [shard_06241_78978]

Contemporary research treats Markov chains both as mathematical objects whose convergence must be understood and as computational mechanisms for exploring distributions that cannot be handled analytically. [shard_04308_30843] [shard_06045_16170]

A finite irreducible and aperiodic chain has a unique stationary distribution, and its distribution after many transitions converges to that stationary distribution regardless of its starting state. [shard_06372_3482]

The mixing time measures how long the chain takes to become approximately stationary, and modern research often studies how that time grows as the underlying graph, combinatorial object, or state space becomes large. [shard_04308_30843] [shard_06372_3482]

Important analytical tools include coupling, eigenvalue and spectral-gap methods, conductance, strong stationary times, and comparisons between random walks and electrical networks. [shard_03951_21465] [shard_06372_3482]

These methods allow researchers to distinguish rapidly mixing chains, which become useful computationally, from chains that remain trapped for long periods in particular regions of the state space. [shard_06372_3482]

In algebraic and enumerative combinatorics, random walks on permutations and groups support the analysis of card shuffling, while random walks on graphs reveal geometric properties such as bottlenecks and expansion. [shard_03951_21465] [shard_04308_30843]

A notable example is riffle shuffling, for which the mixing-time analysis shows that seven shuffles are sufficient to make an ordinary 52-card deck approximately random under a standard distance criterion. [shard_06372_3482]

Markov chains also provide randomized algorithms for approximate counting, including counting graph colourings, where proving a polynomially bounded mixing time supplies a theoretical justification for the algorithm’s efficiency. [shard_06372_3482]

In statistics, Markov chain Monte Carlo constructs a chain whose stationary distribution is the target posterior distribution, allowing expectations and other posterior quantities to be approximated from dependent samples. [shard_06045_16170]

The Metropolis and Metropolis–Hastings algorithms propose moves and accept or reject them so that the resulting chain converges to the desired distribution, while Gibbs sampling updates coordinates from conditional distributions. [shard_06045_16170]

This is especially valuable in Bayesian models whose posterior densities are too complicated to normalize or integrate directly, although high dimensionality, autocorrelation, and slow mixing can make computation difficult. [shard_06045_16170]

Current research therefore focuses not only on constructing chains but also on proving convergence rates, diagnosing dependence, improving simulation algorithms, and handling large or structured state spaces. [shard_00057_20775] [shard_04308_30843]

Applications extend across statistical physics, machine learning, data science, bioinformatics, engineering, random graphs, spin systems, approximate counting, and interacting particle systems. [shard_00057_20775] [shard_04308_30843]

Open directions include sharper results for cutoff and rapid mixing, scalable methods for high-dimensional distributions, non-reversible chains, and principled links with optimal transport, information theory, and convex optimization. [shard_00057_20775]

The expected number of flips needed to obtain N consecutive heads illustrates the Markov-chain method because the relevant state is the current length of the consecutive-head run, not the entire sequence of previous flips. [shard_06398_43597]

Let E_j denote the expected additional number of flips when the current run contains j consecutive heads, for j from 0 through N, with E_N equal to zero because the target has been reached. [shard_06398_43597]

For a coin with head probability p and tail probability q equal to 1 minus p, first-step analysis gives E_j equal to 1 plus pE_{j+1} plus qE_0 for j less than N. [shard_06398_43597]

The term 1 counts the next flip, the pE_{j+1} term describes extending the run after a head, and the qE_0 term describes the complete reset caused by a tail. [shard_06398_43597]

The reset is the key intuition: a tail does not merely remove one head from the current run, because the newly completed suffix contains no consecutive heads and the process returns to state 0. [shard_06398_43597]

Solving these coupled equations gives E_0 equal to (1 minus p to the power N) divided by q times p to the power N. [shard_06398_43597]

For a fair coin, p and q are both one-half, so the expected number of flips is E_0 equal to 2 to the power of N plus 1 minus 2, or equivalently 2 times (2 to the power of N minus 1). [shard_06398_43597]

Consequently, one head requires two flips on average, two consecutive heads require six, three require fourteen, and five require sixty-two. [shard_01901_70670] [shard_02822_24503]

The five-head case can also be represented as an absorbing Markov chain with transient states 0 through 4 and absorbing state 5, where the vector m of expected remaining times satisfies (I minus Q)m equal to the all-ones vector. [shard_02822_24503]

This example shows why Markov chains are useful in statistics and combinatorics: a seemingly history-dependent problem becomes a finite system of linear equations once the state records exactly the information needed for the future. [shard_06398_43597] [shard_02822_24503]
